title: The Letter of Intent Isn't the Sale. The Months After It Decide Whether the Deal Survives.
linkedin:
Most owners relax the moment a letter of intent is signed. That is exactly the wrong moment to relax.

A letter of intent is usually non-binding on price. It is conditional on due diligence, which for most small to mid-market deals runs four to twelve weeks. In that window, a buyer's accountants and lawyers test everything the seller has said about the business, often for the first time.

Here is the specific insight: the business is rarely the problem. The surprise is. Addbacks that made sense to an owner and their bookkeeper don't always hold up when a buyer's accountant asks for evidence behind each one. A customer that looked like one relationship on the P&L turns out to be two contracts with very different renewal terms. None of this means the business is weak. It means it was run for itself, not for a stranger verifying every figure in a six week window.

The outcome owners fear is the deal collapsing. The far more common outcome is retrading, where the buyer comes back partway through and asks for a lower price, an earnout, or extra warranties to cover whatever made them uncomfortable.

A business that has already reconciled its own numbers before it ever goes to market gives a buyer far less room to retrade against. There is nothing left for due diligence to discover that wasn't already disclosed.

If a sale sits somewhere on your horizon, the work that protects the number happens long before the first buyer conversation.

A quick note for any business owner on the East Coast thinking about a sale in the next year or two: the moment that feels like the finish line often isn't one.

Signing a letter of intent feels like relief. In reality, it usually just opens the door to due diligence, the weeks where a buyer's accountants and lawyers test everything that's been said about the business. This is the stage where deals either hold together or get renegotiated down, and it's rarely because the business itself is weak. More often it's addbacks that were never fully substantiated, a customer relationship that turns out to be two contracts with different terms, or management numbers that don't quite reconcile with the tax return.

The businesses that come through this stage cleanly are usually the ones that did the reconciling work before a buyer ever asked for it, not during.

If you're a Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales or Victoria business owner with a sale somewhere on the horizon, it's worth getting your numbers buyer-ready well ahead of time rather than scrambling once an offer is on the table.
